body.hook: In some cultures, it's polite to finish everything on your plate; in others, it suggests the host didn't serve enough. Nobody is born knowing these rules. We learn them, and sociologists call that process socialization.

vocabulary.definition: The shared beliefs, values, behaviours and material objects of a group.
A shared rule or expectation for behaviour.
A shared idea about what is good, right or important.
An informal norm about everyday behaviour (for example, facing forward in an elevator).
A serious norm based on moral views (pronounced "mor-ay").
The lifelong process of learning a culture.
A person or group that teaches us culture, such as family, peers, school or media.

study.title: The Rules Nobody Wrote Down
study.question: How do we learn the culture we live in?
study.passage:
Part 1, Culture inventory (10 minutes): List examples of material culture (objects: smartphones, hockey sticks, bannock, hijabs) and non-material culture (beliefs, language, values, norms) in Canada and in the UAE or another culture you know.
Part 2, Norms ladder (10 minutes): Sort into folkways, mores and laws: saying "thank you"; not cheating on a partner; not stealing; holding a door; not wearing pyjamas to a job interview; not lying to friends. Laws are formal norms enforced by the state.
Part 3, Norm breaking (optional, safe, harmless only, with teacher approval) (10 minutes): Discuss what would happen if you faced the back of an elevator or stood very close to a stranger in line. How do people react? These reactions are informal sanctions.
Part 4, Agents of socialization (15 minutes): For each agent (family, peers, school, media, religion, workplace), write one norm or value it taught you and how.
Part 5, Values compare (5 minutes): Discuss Canadian values (for example multiculturalism, equality, politeness) and values in another culture. Avoid judging one as better: practise cultural relativism.
